posts.title: An emergency fund is not a number. It is a reason.

cover.title: An emergency fund is not a number. It is a reason.
cover.subtitle: How much, where to keep it, and how to start when money is tight.

slides.heading: What it is for
slides.body: Car repair. A dental bill. Two weeks between jobs. It exists so a surprise becomes an inconvenience instead of new debt on a credit card.

slides.heading: The first target
slides.label: covers most everyday surprises
slides.body: Then one month of essentials. Then three to six. The first $500 does the most work, because it breaks the cycle of borrowing for small emergencies.

slides.heading: Where to keep it
items: A separate account, not your checking
A high-yield savings account so it earns something
Boring on purpose: no investing, no lock-ups
Named something like "Emergency" so you hesitate before touching it

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.left: I should pay off all debt before saving anything.
slides.right: A small cushion first. Otherwise the next surprise goes right back on the card.

posts.caption:
An emergency fund is not a number, it is a reason. 🛟 Car repair, dental bill, a gap between paychecks. Without a cushion, every surprise becomes new debt. Start with $500 in a separate high-yield savings account, then build toward one month of essentials. Swipe for where to keep it and the one myth that keeps people from starting ➡️

spec.text: Do not save what is left after spending. Spend what is left after saving.

posts.title: Do not save what is left after spending. Spend what is left after saving.
Interest and APR are two views of the same cost.

slides.heading: Interest is the price of borrowing.
slides.body: When a balance carries past the due date, the card issuer charges interest on it. It is added to the balance, so next month there is a little more to charge interest on.

slides.heading: APR is the yearly rate.
slides.body: APR stands for annual percentage rate. A card at 24% APR charges about 2% a month. Statements show the APR; the interest line shows what that rate cost this month in dollars.

slides.heading: Cards charge daily, not monthly.
slides.body: Most issuers divide the APR by 365 and apply it to the balance every day. That is why paying a few days earlier saves a little, and why a balance grows faster than the yearly rate suggests.

slides.heading: Where to find it on a statement.
slides.body: Look for a box called "Interest Charge Calculation" or "APR." It lists purchase APR, cash advance APR, and any penalty APR. Penalty APRs are often above 29% and can apply after a late payment.

slides.heading: Why it matters.
slides.body: Two people can owe the same $5,000. At 12% APR the interest is about $50 a month at first. At 29% it is about $120. Same balance, very different cost.

posts.caption: Interest and APR describe the same thing from two angles: interest is the dollar cost of carrying a balance, APR is the yearly rate that produces it. Cards apply that rate daily, which is why balances grow faster than people expect and why a penalty APR after one late payment hurts so much. Knowing the APR on each account is the first step to any plan, because it tells you which balance is the most expensive to keep. If you want a clear picture of your own balances, the free review on our site takes about a minute. Link in bio.

spec.fact: Anything you pay above the minimum must go to your highest-APR balance first.
spec.so_what: The CARD Act of 2009. Check a statement and watch it happen.

posts.title: Anything you pay above the minimum must go to your highest-APR balance first.
posts.caption:

posts.title: Five signs the call about your money is a scam.

cover.title: Five signs the call about your money is a scam.
cover.subtitle: They target people who are careful. Especially the careful ones.

slides.heading: The pattern
items: Urgency: act now, today, or else
Payment by gift card, wire, or crypto
A government agency calling out of the blue
A request to keep it secret or stay on the line
Pressure to "verify" a password or full card number

slides.heading: The IRS does not call
slides.body: Neither does Social Security, Medicare, or your bank's fraud team, to demand payment or a code on the spot. They write. You call back on the number printed on your card or statement.

slides.heading: The one move that beats all of them
slides.body: Hang up. Wait ten minutes. Call the organization back using a number you find yourself. Scams depend on not giving you that gap.

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.left: I would never fall for that.
slides.right: Victims skew educated and careful. The scripts are built for smart people under pressure.

posts.caption:
Five signs the call about your money is a scam. 🚩 Urgency, payment by gift card or wire, a government agency calling out of the blue, a request to keep it secret, and pressure to verify a password or full card number. The move that beats all of them: hang up, wait ten minutes, call back on a number you find yourself. Save this for someone you love.

spec.summary: Ronald Read pumped gas and swept floors, drove a used car, and bought dividend-paying stocks he held for decades. When he died in 2014 at 92, he left most of it to his local library and hospital.
spec.source: Reported by CNBC and The Wall Street Journal, 2015

posts.title: A Vermont janitor quietly built an $8 million fortune.
posts.caption:
True story. 🧹 Ronald Read worked as a gas station attendant and a janitor in Brattleboro, Vermont. He drove a used Toyota, chopped his own firewood, and bought shares in companies he understood, then held them for decades. When he died in 2014 at 92 he left about $8 million, most of it to the town library and hospital. No lottery, no inheritance. Time, patience, and living below his means. Source: CNBC, Wall Street Journal (2015).

cover.title: $200 a month can become $243,994. Or $34,617. The difference is time.
cover.subtitle: Same money, same rate. Only the start date changed.

slides.heading: $200 a month at a 7% average return
slides.note: Over 30 years you put in $72,000. The rest is growth on growth.

slides.heading: Why the curve bends
slides.body: Growth earns growth. In year one the interest is small. By year twenty, the money the money made is earning more than you deposit.

slides.heading: It works the same way against you
slides.body: A credit card at 24% compounds daily in the other direction. The same math that builds a retirement account is what makes a balance feel stuck.

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.left: It is too late for me to start.
slides.right: Ten years still turns $24,000 of deposits into about $34,617. The best time was 20 years ago. The next best is this month.

posts.caption:
$200 a month at a 7% average return: about $34,617 after 10 years, $104,185 after 20, $243,994 after 30. 📈 Same money, same rate, only the start date changed. Compound growth is slow at first and then it is not. And it runs the same way against you on a 24% credit card. Swipe for the math ➡️ (Illustration only, not investment advice. Returns vary.)

cover.title: 50 / 30 / 20 is a starting point, not a rule.
cover.subtitle: Needs, wants, future. Here is how to use it without hating it.

bars.label: Future: savings and extra debt payments

slides.heading: Needs first
slides.body: Rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, insurance, transportation, and the minimum on every debt. If needs alone are above 50%, that is information, not failure.

slides.heading: The 20% is the point
slides.body: Emergency fund first, then the highest-interest debt, then retirement. When needs run high, shrink wants before shrinking this slice.

slides.heading: Make it stick
items: Track for one month before changing anything
Automate the 20% on payday
Give wants a real number, not "less"
Review once a month, ten minutes

posts.caption:
50/30/20 is a starting point, not a rule. 🧾 Half of take-home pay to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to the future (emergency fund, extra debt payments, retirement). If your needs are above 50%, that is information, not failure. The 20% is the point: automate it on payday so it never gets a vote. Swipe ➡️

cover.title: A 401(k) match is a raise you have to opt into.
cover.subtitle: What it is, what it is worth, and the one mistake that forfeits it.

slides.heading: A common match
slides.label: a year on a $50,000 salary with a 6% match
slides.body: Contribute 6%, the employer adds 6%. Contribute less and the difference is simply not paid to you.

slides.heading: That match, invested at 7% for 25 years
slides.note: Two piles, one of them free. Illustration only; returns vary.

slides.heading: Vesting
slides.body: Some employers keep part of the match if you leave within a few years. Ask HR for the vesting schedule. It can change the math on switching jobs.

slides.heading: If money is tight
items: Contribute at least enough to get the full match
Raise it 1% each time you get a raise
Do not cash it out when you change jobs; roll it over
Check the fees on the funds once a year

posts.caption:
A 401(k) match is a raise you have to opt into. 💼 On a $50,000 salary with a 6% match, that is $3,000 a year the employer adds only if you contribute. Invested at a 7% average for 25 years, the match alone grows to roughly $202,518. Contribute less than the match and that money is never paid to you.  (Illustration only, not investment advice.)

posts.title: Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score.

cover.title: Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score.
cover.subtitle: It has no memory. Change it and the score reacts next month.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.label: = $3,000 owed on a $10,000 limit
slides.body: Balance divided by limit. Scoring models look at each card and at all cards combined.

slides.heading: Why it counts so much
slides.body: Amounts owed are roughly a third of a FICO score, and utilization is most of that. High utilization signals strain even when every payment is on time.

slides.heading: The common guidance
items: Under 30% is the usual rule of thumb
Under 10% scores better still
One maxed-out card can drag the score even if the overall ratio is fine
Pay before the statement date to lower the reported number

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.left: Closing a paid-off card helps my score.
slides.right: It removes that card's limit from the total, which raises utilization. Keep it open at zero.

posts.caption:
Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score. 📈 Balance divided by limit, per card and overall. Under 30% is the usual rule; under 10% is better. It has no memory: lower the reported balance and the score reacts next cycle. One trap: closing a paid-off card can raise your utilization. Swipe ➡️

cover.title: Most bills are negotiable. Almost nobody asks.
cover.subtitle: A script that works for medical bills, cable, insurance, and card rates.

slides.heading: The four-line script
items: "I have been a customer for X years."
"I am looking at my options and this is higher than I expected."
"Is there a promotion, a hardship rate, or a lower plan?"
"Can you send that in writing?"

slides.heading: Medical bills
slides.body: Ask for an itemized bill, check it against the insurer's statement, then ask about financial assistance and a no-interest payment plan. Errors and discounts are both common.

slides.heading: Card interest rates
slides.body: Call and ask for a lower APR, especially with a good payment history. The worst answer is no. Ask again in six months.

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.right: Retention departments exist because asking works. Polite, specific, and in writing.

posts.caption:
Most bills are negotiable. Almost nobody asks. ☎️ Medical bills, cable, insurance, even your card's interest rate. The script: how long you have been a customer, that the price is higher than expected, whether there is a promotion or lower plan, and can they put it in writing. bubble.text: Minimum due: $150. Easy.

slides.heading: How the minimum is set

slides.heading: Paying only the minimum

Pick a payment and never lower it

Watch the balance, not the minimum

Avalanche pays the highest rate first. Snowball pays the smallest balance first.

cover.title: Avalanche pays the highest rate first. Snowball pays the smallest balance first.
cover.subtitle: Which one wins? The one you keep doing.

slides.heading: The setup is the same
items: List every balance with its APR
Pay the minimum on all of them
Send every extra dollar to one target
When it is gone, roll that payment to the next

slides.heading: Two orders
slides.left: Avalanche: highest APR first. Least interest paid, finishes soonest on paper.
slides.right: Snowball: smallest balance first. A bit more interest, but every closed account is a visible win.

slides.heading: A hybrid that works
slides.body: Close one or two tiny balances first for momentum, then switch to highest rate. The cost difference is usually small. The consistency is what matters.

slides.heading: Either one beats
slides.label: extra dollars spread thinly across every card
slides.body: Focus is the whole trick. Pick a target, aim everything at it, repeat.

posts.caption:
Avalanche or snowball? The right answer is the one you will actually keep doing. ❄️🏔️ Avalanche: highest APR first, least interest paid. Snowball: smallest balance first, fastest visible wins. Either one beats spreading extra money thinly across every card. Swipe for the setup ➡️

slides.heading: Ask for it in writing. Then decide.

Christmas is not an emergency. Neither are tires.

cover.title: Christmas is not an emergency. Neither are tires.
cover.subtitle: Sinking funds: the calm way to handle bills you already know are coming.

slides.heading: What a sinking fund is
slides.body: A small monthly amount set aside for an expense you can see coming: holidays, car maintenance, insurance premiums, a vacation. The bill arrives and the money is already there.

slides.heading: The math
slides.label: a month = $1,200 for the holidays, stress-free
slides.body: Divide the yearly cost by twelve. Automate the transfer. Stop borrowing from the emergency fund for things that were never emergencies.

slides.heading: Common sinking funds
items: Car repairs and registration
Annual insurance premiums
Holidays and birthdays
Medical deductible
Home and appliance repairs

slides.heading: Myth vs fact
slides.left: That is just savings with extra steps.
slides.right: The extra step is the point. A named jar with a date does not get raided.

posts.caption:
Christmas is not an emergency. Neither are tires. 🎄🛞 A sinking fund is a small monthly amount set aside for a bill you can already see coming. $100 a month is $1,200 in December with no card. Divide the yearly cost by twelve, automate it, and stop raiding the emergency fund for things that were never emergencies. Swipe ➡️

cover.title: Buck closes a card.
cover.subtitle: The paid-off card that was quietly helping his score.

bubble.text: Paid off! Closing it so I’m never tempted again.
My score went DOWN?
Same balances. Less total limit. My utilization went up.
Next time: keep it open, one small charge, autopay in full.
Utilization has no memory. Next month’s balance is next month’s score.

slides.heading: Keep paid-off cards open.
slides.body: Utilization is balance divided by limit, across all your cards. Closing a card removes its limit and raises the ratio. Keep it open at zero, or with one small autopaid charge.

posts.caption:
Buck closes a card. ✂️ He paid it off, closed it, and his score dropped. Utilization is balance divided by limit across all cards: $3,000 on $10,000 is 30%, but close a $4,000 card and the same $3,000 is now 50%. Keep paid-off cards open with one small autopaid charge. Utilization has no memory, so the fix shows up next cycle. Swipe ➡️

cover.title: Your credit score is five numbers pretending to be one.
cover.subtitle: What actually moves it, in order of weight.

slides.heading: What FICO weighs
slides.note: New credit and credit mix make up the last 20%.

slides.heading: Payment history
slides.body: One late payment reported 30+ days past due can stay on your report for seven years. Autopay for at least the minimum removes the biggest risk.

slides.heading: Amounts owed
slides.body: Mostly utilization: balance divided by limit, per card and overall. Under 30% is the usual guidance, under 10% is better. This part reacts within a month.

slides.heading: Small things that help
items: Keep old cards open, even at zero
Pay before the statement closes
Dispute errors for free with each bureau
Do not open several new accounts at once

posts.caption:
Your credit score is five numbers pretending to be one. 📊 Payment history is 35% of a FICO score, amounts owed 30%, length of history 15%, and new credit and mix make up the rest. Two of those you can move fast: never miss a payment (autopay the minimum) and keep utilization low. Swipe for the small things that help ➡️

Interest and APR are two views of the same cost.

cover.title: Interest and APR are two views of the same cost.
cover.subtitle: Once you can read them, the statement stops being scary.

slides.heading: Interest is the price of borrowing
slides.body: Carry a balance past the due date and the issuer charges interest on it. It gets added to the balance, so next month there is more to charge.

slides.heading: APR is the yearly rate
slides.label: APR is about 2% a month
slides.body: Statements show the APR. The interest line shows what that rate cost this month, in dollars.

slides.heading: Same $5,000 balance, first month of interest
slides.note: Same balance. Very different cost. The rate matters more than the balance.

slides.heading: Find it on your statement
items: The box labeled Interest Charge Calculation
Purchase APR vs cash advance APR
Any penalty APR, often above 29%
The interest line, in dollars

posts.caption:
Interest and APR are the same cost from two angles. 💳 Interest is the dollar amount, APR is the yearly rate that produces it, applied daily. A $5,000 balance costs about $50 a month at 12% and about $121 at 29%. Knowing the APR on each account tells you which balance is the most expensive to keep. Swipe ➡️

cover.title: A 401(k) match is a raise you have to opt into.
cover.subtitle: What it is, what it is worth, and the one mistake that forfeits it.

slides.heading: A common match
slides.label: a year on a $50,000 salary with a 6% match
slides.body: Contribute 6%, the employer adds 6%. Contribute less and the difference is simply not paid to you.

slides.heading: That match, invested at 7% for 25 years
slides.note: Two piles, one of them free. Illustration only; returns vary.

slides.heading: Vesting
slides.body: Some employers keep part of the match if you leave within a few years. Ask HR for the vesting schedule. It can change the math on switching jobs.

slides.heading: If money is tight
items: Contribute at least enough to get the full match
Raise it 1% each time you get a raise
Do not cash it out when you change jobs; roll it over
Check the fees on the funds once a year

posts.caption:
A 401(k) match is a raise you have to opt into. 💼 On a $50,000 salary with a 6% match, that is $3,000 a year the employer adds only if you contribute. Invested at a 7% average for 25 years, the match alone grows to roughly $202,518. Contribute less than the match and that money is never paid to you. Swipe ➡️ (Illustration only, not investment advice.)

bubble.text: $1,240 for a twenty-minute visit?

slides.heading: Read it. Ask. Then pay.

bubble.text: Car’s making a noise. It’s probably fine.

What if $500 was just sitting there, for exactly this?
$40 a week. Three months. Boring on purpose.

slides.heading: The first $500 does the most work.
slides.body: It turns a surprise into an inconvenience instead of new debt. Keep it in a separate account, named Emergency, and refill it after you use it.

posts.caption:
Buck’s $500 cushion. 🛟 The car noise becomes a $480 repair, and without a cushion it goes on the card at 24%. $40 a week for thirteen weeks is $520 in a separate account named Emergency. The first $500 does the most work of any money you will ever save, because it breaks the cycle of borrowing for small surprises. Swipe ➡️
